strings.title: A Fraction of a Fraction
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Multiplying fractions finds a part of a part: on the area model, the overlap of the two fractions is the product.
strings.keywords: of, part of a part, area model, overlap, numerator times numerator
watchFor: Adding instead of multiplying (1/2 × 1/3 = 2/5): ask "Is a half of a third more or less than a third?"
Thinking multiplying always makes bigger: ask "What is half of a half?"
Cross-multiplying out of habit: draw the area model and count the overlap.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why is 2/3 × 3/4 smaller than both fractions?" Land: it's 2/3 of 3/4, a part of a part. Multiply the numerators for the overlap pieces and the denominators for the size of each piece.

problems.notes: Look for: half of a half. Ask: "What does 1/2 × 1/2 mean?" Word choice: "half of a half". Model: area 1/2 x 1/2

responses.say: Half of a half is a quarter.
responses.tip: The target model.
Added. Ask: are we adding halves, or taking half of a half?

problems.notes: Look for: half of a third. Ask: "How many pieces make the whole now?" Model: area 1/2 x 1/3

responses.say: Half of a third is a sixth.

responses.tip: Added tops and bottoms. Ask: is half of a third more or less than a third?

problems.notes: Look for: 2/6 = 1/3. Ask: "Can you simplify?" Model: area 2/3 x 1/2

responses.tip: Switching the order. Ask: why is it the same?

problems.notes: Look for: 6 of 12 pieces. Ask: "Where is the overlap?" Model: area 2/3 x 3/4

responses.tip: Ask: why 12 pieces?
Connect the rule to the model.
Added. Ask: should 2/3 of 3/4 be more or less than 3/4?

problems.notes: Look for: 12/20 = 3/5. Ask: "Is there a shortcut?" Model: area 3/4 x 4/5

responses.tip: A lovely shortcut. Ask: why does it work?

problems.notes: Look for: 15/30 = 1/2, or 3/6. Ask: "What do you notice about the 5s?" Model: area 5/6 x 3/5
Look for: 1 × 2/3 + 1/2 × 2/3 = 2/3 + 1/3. Ask: "Can you split the mixed number?" Model: area 1 1/2 x 2/3

responses.tip: Improper fractions. Both work.
Multiplied only the fraction parts. Ask: what is 1 × 2/3?

strings.title: Whole Numbers and Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: A whole number times a fraction is repeated groups of that fraction, or that fraction of the whole number.
strings.keywords: groups of, of, repeated addition, unit fraction
watchFor: Multiplying the denominator too (3 × 3/4 = 9/12): ask "Three groups of three quarters: how many quarters?"
Forgetting to rename an improper fraction: ask "How many wholes are in 9/4?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why is 3 × 3/4 the same as 3/4 of 3?" Land: count the unit fractions (3 groups of 3 quarters is 9 quarters), or find the fraction of the whole number.

problems.notes: Look for: three quarters. Ask: "Three groups of a quarter?" Model: numberline +1/4 +1/4 +1/4

responses.tip: Multiplied the bottom too. Ask: how many quarters are there?

problems.notes: Look for: 9 quarters = 2 1/4. Ask: "How many quarters? How many wholes?" Model: numberline +3/4 +3/4 +3/4

responses.tip: The target model.
Ask: is 9/12 more or less than one group of 3/4?

problems.notes: Look for: 12 thirds = 4. Ask: "Is there a quicker way?" Model: numberline +2/3 +2/3 +2/3 +2/3 +2/3 +2/3

responses.tip: Switch the order: 2/3 of 6. Name it.

problems.notes: Look for: 1/3 of 12 is 4, so 2/3 is 8. Ask: "What is one third of 12?" Model: bar 2/3 of 12

responses.say: A third of 12 is 4, two thirds is 8.

responses.tip: Divided by 2. Ask: what is one third of 12?

problems.notes: Look for: 1/4 of 20 is 5, so 3/4 is 15. Ask: "Which unit fraction first?" Model: bar 3/4 of 20

responses.say: A quarter of 20 is 5, three quarters is 15.

responses.tip: All of it minus a quarter.

problems.notes: Look for: 1/6 of 12 is 2, so 5/6 is 10. Ask: "Is it more or less than 12?" Model: bar 5/6 of 12

responses.say: 5/6 of 12: a sixth is 2, five sixths is 10.

problems.notes: Look for: 2 × 4 + 1/2 × 4 = 8 + 2. Ask: "Can you split the mixed number?" Model: area 2 1/2 x 4

responses.tip: Multiplied only the whole. Ask: what is 1/2 × 4?

strings.title: How Many Groups? Dividing by a Fraction
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Dividing by a fraction asks how many of that fraction fit: 3 ÷ 1/4 is how many quarters are in 3.
strings.keywords: how many groups, fit into, quotative division, jumps
watchFor: Thinking division always makes smaller (3 ÷ 1/4 = 3/4): ask "How many quarters fit in 3 wholes?"
Dividing the denominator (3 ÷ 1/4 = 3/4 or 0.75): draw the jumps of 1/4 and count them.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why is 3 ÷ 1/4 bigger than 3?" Land: dividing by a fraction counts how many of that fraction fit in. Small pieces, so many of them.

problems.notes: Look for: how many halves in 2? Four. Ask: "What does ÷ 1/2 mean?" Word choice: "how many halves fit in 2?" Model: numberline +1/2 +1/2 +1/2 +1/2

responses.tip: The target model. Count the jumps.
Took half of 2. Ask: how many halves are in 2?

problems.notes: Look for: 6 halves. Ask: "How does the last problem help?" Model: numberline +1/2 +1/2 +1/2 +1/2 +1/2 +1/2

responses.tip: Took half of 3. Ask: how many halves are in 3?

problems.notes: Look for: 4 quarters in each whole: 12. Ask: "Why is the answer bigger than 3?" Model: numberline +1/4x12

responses.tip: x12 means 12 jumps of 1/4.
Ask: how many quarters fit in 3 wholes?

problems.notes: Look for: three quarters hold 3 quarters. Ask: "How many quarters in 3/4?" Model: numberline +1/4 +1/4 +1/4

responses.tip: Multiplied. Ask: how many quarters fit in three quarters?

problems.notes: Look for: jumps of 2/3 to reach 2: three. Ask: "How many two-thirds fit?" Model: numberline +2/3 +2/3 +2/3

responses.say: 6 thirds in 2, and 2 thirds per group: 6 ÷ 2 = 3.
responses.tip: Common denominators. Nice.
Multiplied. Ask: how many 2/3 jumps reach 2?

problems.notes: Look for: two jumps of 3/4 make 1 1/2. Ask: "How many 3/4s fit?" Model: numberline +3/4 +3/4
Look for: 30 sixths ÷ 5 sixths = 6. Ask: "How many 5/6s fit in 5?" Model: numberline +5/6 +5/6 +5/6 +5/6 +5/6 +5/6

strings.title: Adding and Subtracting Unlike Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Rename fractions as the same-sized pieces before adding or subtracting. The clock (minutes) works for halves, thirds, quarters, sixths and twelfths; for fifths and tenths, use tenths or decimals.
strings.keywords: common denominator, equivalent fractions, clock, twelfths, rename, mixed numbers
watchFor: Adding tops and bottoms (5/6 + 3/4 = 8/10): ask "Is 8/10 more or less than 5/6?"
Renaming only one fraction: ask "Are both the same size of piece now?"
With mixed numbers, taking a big fraction from a small one: ask "Could you count up instead?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What size of piece did you use each time, and why?" Land: find a size both fractions can be made of: twelfths for sixths and quarters, tenths for fifths and halves. Then add or subtract the pieces.

problems.notes: Look for: 50 + 45 = 95 minutes, or 10/12 + 9/12. Ask: "What size of piece?" Word choice: "same-sized pieces". Model: clock 5/6 + 3/4

responses.tip: Added tops and bottoms. Ask: is 8/10 more than 5/6?

problems.notes: Look for: 12/20 − 5/20. Ask: "Does the clock work for fifths?" Model: text 3/5 = 12/20 ; 1/4 = 5/20 ; 12/20 - 5/20 = 7/20

responses.tip: Decimals: 0.35 is 7/20.

problems.notes: Look for: 1/4 to 2, then 1/3: 3/12 + 4/12. Ask: "Count up?" Model: numberline 1 3/4 >2 >2 1/3

responses.tip: Took 1/3 from 3/4. Ask: if you take away more than 1 1/2, can 1 5/12 be left?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 + 1/2 + 2/3 = 3 + 7/6. Ask: "Wholes first?" Model: numberline 1 1/2 +2 +1/2 +1/6
Look for: 7/10 + 5/10 − 6/10. Ask: "What common piece for all three?" Model: text 7/10 + 5/10 - 6/10 = 6/10 = 3/5

responses.tip: As decimals.

strings.title: Adding and Subtracting with Negative Fractions
strings.label: Bank
strings.strategy: Negative fractions and decimals follow the same rules as integers: adding a negative moves down, subtracting is the distance from one to the other. Jump to zero when you cross it.
strings.keywords: rational numbers, negative fractions, zero, direction, distance, number line
watchFor: Dropping the negative sign: ask "Is the answer above or below zero?"
Adding the fractions but using the wrong direction: ask "Up or down from −1/2?"
Getting lost with mixed numbers below zero: ask "How far is −1 1/4 from 0?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How is this like adding and subtracting integers?" Land: it's the same number line. Jump to zero first, then use what's left, and use the same-sized pieces for the fractions.

problems.notes: Look for: up 1/2 to 0, then 1/4. Ask: "Do you cross zero?" Word choice: "negative one half". Model: numberline -1/2 +1/2 +1/4

responses.tip: Added the sizes, kept the sign. Ask: up or down from −1/2?

problems.notes: Look for: up 1/2 doesn't reach zero. Ask: "What's different?" Model: numberline -3/4 +1/2
Look for: down 1/3 to 0, then 2/3 more. Ask: "Below zero?" Model: numberline 1/3 -1/3 -2/3

responses.tip: Ask: is 1/3 − 1 above or below zero?

problems.notes: Look for: down 1/2 more. Ask: "Up or down?" Model: numberline -1 1/4 -1/2
Look for: from −1.25 up to −0.75: 0.5. Ask: "Distance from which to which?" Model: vline -1.25 >-0.75

responses.tip: Added the sizes. Ask: how far apart are −0.75 and −1.25?

problems.notes: Look for: from −1/6 up to 2/3: 1/6 + 2/3. Ask: "How far?" Model: numberline -1/6 >0 >2/3
Look for: up 2 1/2 to 0, then 9/10. Ask: "What's left after zero?" Model: numberline -2 1/2 +2 1/2 +9/10
